To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
EB binds in two modes: electrostatic binding to phosphate groups, and intercalation into base pairs.

EB intercalates in DNA and RNA, but only in base-paired regions; that the number of intercalating sites in DNA is 0.5-0.7 per base pair; that the binding is specific for GC pairs, but is not affected by the secondary structure of the DNA, and that the binding is cooperative, but not cooperative in the sense of cooperativity in melting.
EB forms a fluorescent complex with DNA, RNA and RNA:DNA hybrids, and that this binding is specific for base-pair regions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interaction of the fluorescent dye ethidium bromidewith nucleic acids.
the interaction of ethidium bromides (EB) with nucleic acids, in particular, the binding of EB to double-stranded nucleic acids.
the interaction of a fluorescent cationic dye with polynucleotids.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
EB is intercalated into DNA, with the plane of the molecule parallel to the base pairs, at a distance of approximately 3.4 A from the helix axis, and at a depth of approximately 3 A into the helix.
the binding of EB to DNA is a complex phenomenon, and that the binding of the dye to DNA is not a simple electrostatic interaction.
EB is a specific intercalating dye, and that complex I is a complex of EB and DNA, in which the dye is intercalated between base pairs, with a stoichiometry of 1 EB/2 base pairs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the EB binding sites are the base-paired regions of double-helical DNA, and that the dye intercalates between the base pairs in these regions.
EB intercalates into the DNA helix at high ionic strength and at low pH, but that at low ionic strength the dye binds electrostatically to the DNA.
EB intercalation is a specific process which is sensitive to the base-paired character of the binding sites, and which is strongly affected by the presence of Mg2+.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the binding of EB to nucleic acids involves two distinct modes of binding, which are both intercalative.
EB binds to DNA in two different modes, one of which is highly specific for the base-paired regions of the helix.
EB intercalates between base pairs in DNA, RNA and RNA: DNA hybrids.
